items.title: Texas sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over ChatGPT safety and child protection
items.summary: On Friday 23 October, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman in Collin County district court. The state says OpenAI misrepresented ChatGPT's safety and reliability and failed to warn users of its risks. It claims violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the SCOPE Act, the state's law on protecting children online, including missing age verification. Texas wants $10,000 per violation, the return of profits, and Altman held personally liable. It also asks for an injunction that would block minors from the product and require a court-appointed evaluator to approve new models before release. An OpenAI spokesperson said governments have an important role in setting safety standards. The suit is separate from the eight states that sued on 14 October.
items.why_it_matters: Texas is the ninth state to sue OpenAI in October. Its demand that a court-appointed evaluator approve new models before launch would be a kind of court-run pre-approval regime, one that Congress has never passed.

items.title: UK sets out about £600 million for AI security, including a £100 million AI Biosecurity Lab
items.summary: Ahead of next week's Budget, the UK government announced about £600 million (about $800 million) for AI security. The package includes £100 million for an AI Biosecurity Lab to detect biological threats and £65 million for countermeasures against dangerous pathogens. The AI Security Institute gets another £120 million, and two new cyber programmes (the National Cyber Shield and the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre) get £130 million. OpenAI and Anthropic will provide up to £200 million in model credits, and Google DeepMind and Basecamp Research will also contribute. Smaller items include £60 million for AI in robotics and manufacturing and £18 million for a chip design academy.
items.why_it_matters: The UK is betting its AI policy on security and biosecurity, not regulation, and the AI Security Institute is getting more money. Leading AI labs are now co-financing government security work.

items.title: Anthropic's draft federal AI safety bill draws backlash, and Amodei calls it a possible 'mistake'
items.summary: Politico revealed on 16 October that Anthropic was circulating a draft federal AI safety bill, and wider coverage followed this week. Under the draft, independent evaluators registered with the Commerce Department would assess frontier models. If they found a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than 50 deaths or more than $1 billion in damage from bioweapons, cyberattacks or a model evading its developer's controls, they would have 72 hours to notify Commerce. Commerce would then ask a federal judge in Washington, D.C., to halt the release. No federal agency could stop a model on its own. AI safety groups, led by Nathan Calvin of Encode, criticised the threshold as far too high. On 21 October, Dario Amodei posted a long rebuttal on X, and Inside Defense reported that he said the draft may have been a 'mistake'. No member of Congress has introduced the bill.
items.why_it_matters: An AI lab writing its own draft law shows how much the industry wants to shape US federal rules. The thresholds in the draft show how high the bar for government intervention could end up.

items.title: Judge hears first fair-use arguments over AI training since Bartz and Kadrey, in the music publishers' case against Anthropic
items.summary: On 21 October in San Jose, US District Judge Eumi Lee heard cross-motions for summary judgment in Concord Music Group v. Anthropic (N.D. Cal. 5:24-cv-03811). The plaintiffs include Universal Music Publishing Group, Concord and ABKCO. The publishers say Claude reproduces lyrics, sometimes word for word, and cite about 120,000 prompts used to generate synthetic lyrics that could compete with human songwriters. Anthropic says training on the lyrics is fair use and that Claude is not a substitute for the songs. The judge focused mostly on market harm and took the motions under submission without ruling. Law360 reported that she seemed open to parts of Anthropic's fair-use defence. It is the first time a district judge has weighed fair use for AI training since the Bartz and Kadrey rulings.
items.why_it_matters: The ruling could decide whether this becomes the first AI copyright case to go to trial. It will also be an important precedent on what training on copyrighted works will cost AI companies.

items.title: Record week for AI copyright suits: Canadian news publishers and music companies sue Anthropic
items.summary: On 19 October, The Canadian Press reported that Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press have sued Anthropic in an Ontario court. They say Claude was built on their content without a licence, and that Anthropic breached their websites' terms of service and got around technical protections. One report says they are seeking up to $20,000 in statutory damages per infringed work. The suit was filed on 6 October. The same publishers are already suing OpenAI. On 21 October, Reservoir Media filed separate suits against Anthropic and Suno in the Northern District of California. The ChatGPT Is Eating the World tracker counted eight new AI copyright suits that week, a four-year record, bringing its total to 156.
items.why_it_matters: Copyright suits are piling up across countries and industries. That raises the legal risk and licensing costs for AI companies and strengthens media companies' bargaining position.

items.title: UK FCA: financial firms must report significant AI failures and near-misses
items.summary: Speaking on Monday 19 October at the Bloomberg UK Policy Series, Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, said the existing rules on reporting major incidents must also cover 'significant AI failures and near-misses'. She called near-miss reporting for agentic AI a regulatory and national-security priority. She also said agentic systems need 'continuous, conditional assurance', and that the FCA will work with industry, other regulators and frontier labs on a framework for 'agentic finance'. The FCA has not defined 'significant' or 'near-miss'.
items.why_it_matters: This directly affects banks and finance firms using AI agents. Supervisors expect incident reporting and logging for AI now, before any new AI-specific rules are in place.

items.title: Court orders Meta to name the people behind its book torrenting for AI training
items.summary: US Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixson (N.D. Cal.) issued a discovery order requiring Meta to identify the people who made, authorised or approved decisions to download shadow-library datasets such as Anna's Archive and LibGen via BitTorrent, and decisions about seeding. The order applies to the authors' class action Kadrey v. Meta and to Entrepreneur Media's suit. Meta had said it knew of no one who had approved distribution. Meta is accused of downloading more than 81 TB from Anna's Archive. Sources date the order to 19 or 20 October. It does not decide liability.
items.why_it_matters: How AI companies obtained their training data, rather than the training itself, is becoming their biggest legal exposure. That includes possible personal responsibility for executives.

items.title: Former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an executive conference room is held without bail
items.summary: On 19 October, federal judge Alex Tse in San Francisco ordered Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national and former OpenAI engineer, held without bail as a flight risk. He is charged with using a device to intercept oral communications and faces up to five years in prison. Prosecutors say he hid a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room (it was found on 30 September), that he was 'mere days' from fleeing to Saudi Arabia, and that he was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi royal family who tried to recruit him to an AI venture. The investigation is ongoing and may lead to more charges. On 16 October, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton cited the case as a threat to US AI leadership.
items.why_it_matters: The case shows that physical security and insider risk at frontier labs are now treated as national security. That can lead to stricter security requirements for AI companies.

items.title: Meta revises its commercial terms, but lawyers say they still allow broad scraping of websites
items.summary: Ahead of new commercial terms taking effect on 30 October, Meta removed the word 'train' from the disputed clause and limited the crawling provision to its 'advertising and business products'. Meta says publishers can still control crawling with robots.txt. Legal experts quoted by Nieman Lab and others say the terms still give broad scraping rights that could override robots.txt, because the terms do not mention robots.txt and the word 'develop' could cover AI training. Business accounts cannot opt out before the terms take effect.
items.why_it_matters: Contract terms are becoming a new battleground over AI training data. Companies that advertise with Meta may be giving away rights to their own content without realising it.
